title: Heirs in dhamma
hook: be my heirs in the teaching, not in material things (MN 3)

segments.voice: Yesterday: wise attention, and your line, the useful question. When a question started looping, did you swap it for what would ease this? Day four hundred five.

Families can fight over the strangest things after a funeral. Not only the house or the savings. The good china. A watch. A recipe card in a grandmother's handwriting. What we inherit says something about who we were to the person who left. The Buddha, very much alive, once told his monks exactly what he wanted them to inherit from him, and then gave an example to show he meant it. Today: heirs in dhamma.
screen: `THE CHINA, THE WATCH, THE RECIPE CARD.` → `WHAT WILL YOU INHERIT?`

segments.voice: MN 3, the Dhammadayada. It opens with one line: monks, be my heirs in the teaching, not my heirs in material things. The word for material things is amisa: flesh, food, the things of the body, and sometimes bait. Then the Buddha makes it concrete. Suppose, he says, I've eaten and finished my meal, and some food is left over, about to be thrown away. Two monks arrive, hungry and weak. I tell them: here is leftover food; eat it if you want, otherwise I'll throw it out. The first monk thinks: the Teacher said be heirs in the teaching, not in material things, and this food is a material thing. So he goes without, and spends the night hungry and weak. The second monk eats, and spends the night comfortably. And the Buddha says the first monk is the one more to be honored. Why? He says it will lead, for a long time, to fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, ease in supporting oneself, and energy. It can be an uncomfortable example to hear. The point isn't that food is bad; the example opens with the Buddha finishing his own meal. The point is what you reach for when something is offered, and what that habit hands down. Then the Buddha gets up and goes into his dwelling, and Sariputta takes over, teaching how a teacher's disciples train in seclusion, or fail to. The Dhammapada puts the value plainly, in Max Müller's translation: “The gift of the law exceeds all gifts.”
screen: `HEIRS IN TEACHING, NOT THINGS.` · `AMISA — FOOD, FLESH, BAIT.` · `TWO HUNGRY MONKS, ONE MEAL.` · `THE GIFT OF THE LAW.` · then, large: `INHERIT THE TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one thing you're holding onto that is only material: a purchase you keep circling, a comfort you reach for out of habit. Imagine setting it down, just for today. Now pick up one teaching from the last weeks to carry instead: the post holds, your own ground, seven ways, the useful question. Hold that one for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Dhamma-dayada, heir in the teaching. The Buddha's wish that his followers inherit his teaching, not his material things.
Your line: inherit the teaching. Today, pass on one thing you've learned to someone, instead of something you've bought. Day four hundred five.

howItsDone: Buddhists often cite the Dhammapada line that the gift of the teaching exceeds all gifts, and in some communities giving or sponsoring copies of the teachings, or teaching others, is counted as a gift of dhamma.

myth: MN 3 teaches that food is evil
the example opens with the Buddha's own meal; the point is what you reach for and hand down.
the Buddha calls the monk who went hungry more to be honored
for the sake of fewness of wishes and contentment.
flesh, food, worldly things, and the lure on a hook.

fork.setup: you're a hungry, weak monk. the Buddha offers you food he's about to throw away. what does the first monk in MN 3 do?
options: goes without, remembering 'heirs in the teaching'
fork.reveal: he goes hungry that night, and the Buddha says he's the one more to be honored. the second monk, who ate, did nothing wrong; the story is about what each chose to carry forward.

original.note: Pali dhamma-dāyāda: heir in the dhamma, the teaching.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule about not eating leftovers.
what it means: carry forward the teaching, not the comforts: few wishes and a contented mind.
what a scholar hears: dhamma and āmisa form a recurring pair; elsewhere the suttas speak of two kinds of gift, of things and of dhamma, and call the gift of dhamma foremost.
